vignette:
Session Notes – Patient #2217

He comes in still wearing his duty jacket, the Coast Guard patch frayed at the edges from salt and sun. He sits on the edge of the chair, not quite comfortable, not quite ready to leave. He’s twenty-nine, in a steady relationship with a woman named Elise who works in a dental office, and he tells me he’s been having trouble sleeping for about eight months now. He doesn't say "since the robbery." He says "since things got weird."

The story comes out in pieces, like wreckage washing ashore.

It happened on a Tuesday night in late February. He’d just finished a double shift at the station on the coast, helping with a medevac off a fishing trawler. He was tired, but wired, the way he gets after a rescue. He stopped at a convenience store near his apartment to get milk and a protein bar. He was walking back to his truck in the dim lot when two men came around the corner of the building. He remembers one of them had a hood pulled so tight it flattened his nose. The other had a knife—not a big one, but sharp, held low and steady.

They wanted his wallet. He gave it. They wanted his phone. He gave that too. Then one of them said something about his jacket, the blue one with the Coast Guard emblem, and told him to take it off. He hesitated. That half-second felt like an hour. The one with the knife stepped forward and pressed the tip into the soft skin just below his ribs. He remembers the cold, the precise pressure, the way his breath stopped.

He took off the jacket. They ran. He stood there in the parking lot in the February cold, wearing only a t-shirt, holding a protein bar, watching them disappear into the dark between streetlights.

He didn't call the police. He drove home. He told Elise he’d been mugged, and she made him file a report the next morning. The officers were polite, took his statement, said they’d look into it. They never found the men.

That was eight months ago. He still hasn't bought a new jacket. He wears a different one now, a black windbreaker, but he says it doesn't feel right. He keeps the old one in the back of his closet, still stained with a little bit of mud from the parking lot, because he can't bring himself to throw it away.

At work, he’s fine. He has to be. When the call comes in, he moves. He’s done three major rescues since the robbery, pulled a hypothermic kayaker out of the water, helped stabilize a man having a heart attack on a cargo ship. His crewmates don't know. He doesn't talk about it. But he's started checking the parking lot every time he leaves the station. He walks to his truck with his keys between his fingers, scanning the edges of the light. He doesn't go to the convenience store anymore. He drives an extra ten minutes to a different one, and even then, he only goes during daylight.

The worst part, he says, is not the fear. He’s used to fear. Fear is part of the job. The worst part is the shame. He was a Coast Guardsman. He was supposed to be the one who helps. And he just stood there, shivering in a t-shirt, handing over his things. He replays that half-second hesitation over and over—the moment he didn't fight, didn't run, didn't do anything. He tells me he feels like a coward. He doesn't say this with anger. He says it quietly, like a fact he's been carrying.

He's been drinking more. Not a lot, but more than he used to. A beer or two before bed to take the edge off. Elise has noticed he's jumpy. She asked him the other night if he was okay, and he snapped at her. He still feels bad about it. He says she’s been patient, but he can see the worry in her eyes, and he doesn't know how to explain something he can't even name.

He doesn't have nightmares about the robbery. He has nightmares about the water. In the dream, he's in the water, and he can't find the boat, and his hands are too cold to hold onto anything. He wakes up gasping, his heart pounding, convinced for a moment that he's drowning. He doesn't know why that dream started. He's never been afraid of the water. He's a rescue swimmer. The water is where he belongs.

He's here today because Elise made the appointment. He didn't argue. He says he doesn't know if this will help, but he's tired. He's just really, really tired.
